items.title: Comparing and advising
items.goal: Compare with daha, en and kadar, and use indefinite pronouns.

blocks.text: The comparative is formed with daha (more) before the adjective: daha büyük (bigger). The point of comparison takes the ablative: Ali'den daha uzun (taller than Ali).

To give advice, you can use <tur>bence</tur> (in my opinion), <tur>-meli</tur> (you should) or <tur>istersen</tur> (if you want): <tur>Bence dinlenmelisin.</tur> (In my opinion, you should rest.), <tur>İstersen yardım edebilirim.</tur> (If you want, I can help.).

<tur>herkes</tur> (everyone), <tur>kimse</tur> (nobody), <tur>hiç kimse</tur> (absolutely nobody), <tur>bir şey</tur> (something), <tur>hiçbir şey</tur> (nothing), <tur>her şey</tur> (everything), <tur>bazıları</tur> (some people).

items.fr: I am better today.
This is the most beautiful city in the world.
Can you run as fast as me?
Everyone can learn Turkish.

blocks.text: After a comparative adjective, the point of comparison goes in the ablative: <tur>benden daha genç</tur> (younger than me). Do not translate «than» as a separate word.

quiz.why: The comparative is formed with daha: daha büyük.

items.title: Ability, passive, causative
items.goal: Express ability, form the passive and have something done.

blocks.text: The ability form is built with -ebil / -abil between the root and the ending: konuşabilirim (I can speak). The negative form is irregular: konuşamam (I cannot speak).

The passive is marked with -il / -in / -n: yazılmak (to be written), açılmak (to be opened), soyulmak (to be burgled). The causative adds -dir / -t / -ir: yaptırmak (to have something done), kestirmek (to have something cut).
-ecekti / -acaktı expresses an action that was planned in the past: Dün gelecektim ama işim çıktı. (I was supposed to come yesterday, but something came up.).

items.fr: Can you speak Turkish? — I can speak a little.
The car was repaired.
I had my hair cut.
I was supposed to come yesterday, but something came up.

blocks.text: With a long verb, look for the blocks: <tur>yap-tır-ıl-dı</tur> = causative + passive + past: «it was caused to be done». Break it down from right to left.

vocab: to go out, to come up

quiz.q: How do you say «I can speak»?
quiz.why: The affirmative ability form uses -abil: konuş- + -abil + -irim.
The passive -il turns «to open» into «to be opened»: açıldı.

items.title: Past continuous and culture
items.goal: Combine past tenses, understand proverbs and discover Atatürk.

blocks.text: The past continuous (-yordu) describes an action in progress in the past: geliyordum (I was coming). The past perfect (-mişti) marks an action that happened before another past moment: gelmiştim (I had already come).

items.fr: We were about to go out when it started to rain.
When he arrived, I had already fallen asleep.
As children, we used to go to the sea every summer.

blocks.text: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (1881–1938) is the founder of the Republic of Turkey, proclaimed in 1923. He launched major reforms: adoption of the Latin alphabet in 1928, expansion of education, political rights for women (the right to stand for election in 1934) and modernisation of the country. His name remains associated with secularism and national sovereignty.

quiz.q: Which sentence means «we were going out»?
quiz.why: The past continuous -yordu expresses an action in progress: çıkıyorduk.
-mişti is the past perfect: an action completed before another past moment.

items.title: At the doctor's
items.goal: Describe your symptoms, understand the doctor's questions and follow a prescription.

blocks.text: To say where it hurts, the body part takes the possessive and the verb ağrımak stays in the third person: başım ağrıyor (word for word: my head hurts). For a fever, you use var: ateşim var (I have a fever).
The doctor's questions

blocks.caption: What the doctor asks
head: Question
Translation
rows: What seems to be the problem?
Are you allergic to any medication?

items.tr: Kendimi iyi hissetmiyorum, başım ağrıyor ve ateşim var.
items.fr: I don't feel well, I have a headache and a fever.

items.tr: Ne zamandan beri böyle? — Dünden beri.
items.fr: Since when have you been like this? — Since yesterday.

items.tr: İlaçlara alerjiniz var mı? — Hayır, yok.
items.fr: Are you allergic to any medication? — No.

items.tr: Çok geçmiş olsun, umarım yakında iyileşirsiniz.
items.fr: Wishing you a speedy recovery, I hope you feel better soon.

blocks.text: Understanding the prescription

blocks.caption: The doctor's instructions
head: Turkish
Meaning
rows: Twice a day, after a meal
Half an hour before a meal
Rest, do not go to work
If it does not go away, come back

blocks.text: The conditional instruction combines -mezse (if it does not happen) and the polite imperative: Eğer ateşiniz geçmezse, yarın tekrar gelin. (If your fever does not go away, come back tomorrow.).

The body part takes the possessive: <tur>baş-ım</tur>, <tur>karın-ım</tur>, <tur>boğaz-ım</tur>, <tur>diş-im</tur>. The verb <tur>ağrımak</tur> is not conjugated with «I»: you say <tur>dişim ağrıyor</tur>, never <tur>ben ağrıyorum</tur>.

<tur>Geçmiş olsun</tur> is said to someone who is ill or after an accident. The usual reply is <tur>Teşekkür ederim</tur> or <tur>Sağ olun</tur>. The polite «you» is expected with the doctor: <tur>Neyiniz var?</tur>, not <tur>Neyin var?</tur>.

quiz.q: How do you say «I have a headache»?
quiz.why: The body part takes the possessive and ağrımak stays in the third person: başım ağrıyor.

quiz.q: What does «Günde iki kez, yemekten sonra» mean?
options: Twice a day, after a meal
Twice a week, before a meal
Once a day, on an empty stomach
quiz.why: günde iki kez = twice a day; yemekten sonra = after a meal.

items.title: On the phone and at public offices
items.goal: Make phone calls, leave a message and understand the formal register of official procedures.

blocks.text: On the phone, you answer with <tur>Alo</tur> or <tur>Buyurun</tur> (I'm listening). To ask for someone: <tur>Kimi arıyorsunuz?</tur> (Who are you calling?). If the person is unavailable: <tur>Şu anda müsait değil.</tur> (They are not available at the moment.).

blocks.caption: Phone phrases
head: Turkish
Meaning
rows: May I speak to Mr Ali?
He is busy at the moment.
Would you like to leave a message?

blocks.text: In administrative settings, the register is more formal. You often add -dır / -dir to state a fact neutrally: Aradığınız numara yanlıştır. (The number you have called is incorrect.), Randevunuz onaylanmıştır. (Your appointment is confirmed.).

Polite requests are formed with -abilir misiniz?: Mesajımı iletir misiniz? (Could you pass on my message?), Beni bağlayabilir misiniz? (Could you put me through?), Biraz daha yavaş konuşabilir misiniz? (Could you speak a little more slowly?).

items.tr: Alo, buyurun. — Merhaba, Ayşe Hanım'la görüşebilir miyim?
items.fr: Hello, I'm listening. — Hello, may I speak to Mrs Ayşe?

items.tr: Şu anda toplantıda, mesaj bırakmak ister misiniz?
items.fr: She is in a meeting at the moment, would you like to leave a message?

items.tr: Aradığınız numara yanlıştır, lütfen kontrol ediniz.
items.fr: The number you have called is incorrect, please check it.

items.tr: Kayıt için kimlik belgenizi gösterebilir misiniz?
items.fr: For registration, could you show your ID?
Could you speak a little more slowly?

blocks.text: On the phone, Turkish prefers short formulas: <tur>Buyurun</tur> replaces «hello», and <tur>Bir dakika</tur> is enough to ask someone to wait. Do not translate French word for word.
-dır is used in the administrative register, but it can also express a deduction: Şu anda evdedir. (He must be at home.). Context decides.
<tur>Yanlış numara</tur> is correct but blunt. The full formula <tur>Aradığınız numara yanlıştır, özür dilerim.</tur> is more polite.

quiz.q: What do you say when you answer the phone?
quiz.why: Buyurun politely invites the other person to speak; güle güle is used to say goodbye.

options: The number you have called is incorrect
quiz.why: yanlış = wrong, incorrect; here the suffix -dır gives an administrative tone.
